html:
Two dynasties that in turn ruled the Deccan, the plateau of central and southern India, from 543 to the late 10th century. The Chalukyas ruled first, from Badami; the Rashtrakutas overthrew them and ruled from Manyakheta.

The Chalukyas of Badami (543 to 753). Pulakeshin I founded the dynasty at Vatapi, modern Badami, in Karnataka. His grandson Pulakeshin II stopped the northern emperor Harsha at the Narmada river, but lost his life and his capital to the Pallavas in 642. The dynasty recovered. Its temples at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal mix northern and southern styles and are early landmarks of Indian stone architecture.

The Rashtrakutas (753 to about 982). In 753 the governor Dantidurga overthrew his Chalukya overlords. His successor Krishna I had the Kailasa temple at Ellora carved down into a hillside from a single mass of rock, one of the largest monolithic structures ever made.

At its height the Rashtrakuta empire reached from the Ganges plain to the far south:

  • Its kings raided north to Kannauj, the prize in a three-way struggle with the Palas of Bengal and the Gurjara-Pratiharas.
  • Amoghavarsha I (814 to 878) ruled for over sixty years. An early work on Kannada poetics is credited to him, and an Arab merchant counted him among the four great kings of the world.
  • Krishna III defeated the Cholas at Takkolam in 949.

In 973 a Chalukya descendant, Tailapa II, overthrew the last strong Rashtrakuta king and founded the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani. A final Rashtrakuta claimant died in 982.
sum: Two dynasties that in turn ruled the Deccan, the plateau of central and southern India, from 543 to the late 10th century. The Chalukyas ruled first, from Badami; the Rashtrakutas overthrew them and ruled from Manyakheta.
